# Egashira et al., TestSuiteBench: generating test suites from specifications

**Source:** Kazuki Egashira, Niels Mündler-Sasahara, Mark Niklas Müller, Martin Vechev (ETH Zurich; LogicStar.ai). *TestSuiteBench: Coding Agents Struggle to Generate Strong Test Suites from Specifications*. ## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The authors argue that coding agents have moved from resolving isolated issues to re-implementing complex applications such as a C compiler and a web browser, which suggests that fully autonomous development of genuinely new software is within reach (§1, "Introduction") [AR]. Such development, they argue, depends on strong verification of the agent's work against intended behaviour; re-implementations can lean on existing test suites and reference implementations, but genuinely new software starts with only a natural-language specification, so the agent must be able to turn that specification into a strong test suite (§1, "Introduction") [AR]. Existing benchmarks do not measure this: code-generation benchmarks have scaled to complete applications, while test-generation benchmarks remain limited to individual issues, a few files or single scenarios, and always provide the implementation to test (§1, "Introduction") [AR].

Their answer is TestSuiteBench, a benchmark of 165 open-source applications, each with a structured and detailed specification, a reference implementation, a reference test suite and on average 74 mutants; each mutant is generated from a single requirement and refined to isolate it, so that 73% are killed by exactly one reference test and, on average, by only 0.2% of the remaining tests (Abstract) [AE]. An agent receives only the natural-language specification and must write a full test suite, which is scored by its validity (the fraction of its tests that pass on the reference implementation) and its mutation score (the fraction of mutants its valid tests kill) (§1, "Our work"; Figure 1 caption) [AP].

Across coding agents built on six recent frontier models, the best suite (Claude Opus 5) kills 55.5% of mutants and four of the six agents stay below 40%, while four of the six agents write tests that are 88-96% valid and implementations built from the same specifications pass up to 93% of the reference tests (§1, "Introduction"; §3.1, "Main Results"; Table 2) [AE]. Giving GPT 5.6 Sol the reference executable alongside the specification raised its validity rate but left its mutation score at about 38% (§3.2, "Providing Reference Executables for Test Generation"; Table 4) [AE]. From these results the authors conclude that the bottleneck is test design rather than specification precision, and that generated suites are often too small and miss the input combinations needed to expose violated requirements (§1, "Introduction"; §6, "Conclusion") [AR]:

> "These results reveal a critical gap: agents can build software they cannot verify. Until they can turn
> specifications into strong test suites, fully autonomous development of new software remains out of
> reach" (§1, "Introduction") [V]

The authors bound the claim themselves: mutants are a proxy for test strength and need not reflect real-world faults, their specifications are more detailed than typical developer documentation (which may make the evaluation overestimate agents), all artefacts inherit the reference implementation's bugs, and the benchmark covers only command-line applications in compiled languages (§5, "Limitations and Future Work") [AP]. The paper is a preprint; its reproducibility statement says the full benchmark data and code will be released upon publication (Reproducibility Statement) [AP].

## Part I: The problem and the benchmark's framing

### The verification gap

The introduction places the work in a progression: coding agents went from resolving isolated issues (citing Yang et al., 2024) to use across the software engineering lifecycle (citing Mürtz & Müller, 2025; Huang et al., 2026), and have re-implemented complex applications from scratch with little human involvement, including a C compiler and a web browser (citing Carlini, 2026; Lin, 2026) (§1, "Introduction") [BT]. The authors note that such systems took human teams years to build (§1, "Introduction") [AP].

They then argue that autonomous development depends on strong verification that checks an agent's work against intended behaviour (citing Carlini, 2026), and that for genuinely new software the verification material available to re-implementations, existing test suites and reference implementations, does not exist (§1, "Introduction") [AR]. The agent must therefore verify its implementation against the specification by translating it into a strong test suite (§1, "Introduction") [AR].

### Why such a benchmark is hard to build

The authors name two difficulties. Ambiguity, inconsistency and incompleteness of natural language are a main source of software testing errors (citing Mustafa et al., 2021) [BT], and measuring a test suite's strength needs faults that violate specific requirements, "which generic rule-based mutations cannot guarantee" (§1, "Introduction") [V], citing Jia & Harman (2011) [BT].

### Notation and the kill relation

The paper writes a repository R as holding a reference implementation I∗, from which a build script produces a reference executable E∗, and a reference test suite T∗ that validates both; starred artefacts are references and hatted ones (T̂, Î) are under evaluation (§2, "Notation") [AP]. A test suite can be seen as an executable verifier of the alignment between an executable E and a natural-language specification S; mutants M are executables with specific defects with respect to S, used to assess a suite's strength (§2, "Notation") [AP].

A test or suite kills an executable if the test fails when processing it, and the authors set the target for a suite: "A high quality test suite never kills the reference executable" while killing all mutants (§2, "Notation") [V]. Because the reference suite kills every mutant, a perfect score is attainable by construction (§1, "Our work") [AP].

### Key contributions as the authors list them

The authors claim three contributions: the benchmark itself, for repository-scale test-suite generation from natural-language specifications (165 applications with specifications, reference implementations, reference suites and requirement-targeted mutants); a scalable pipeline that derives specifications from existing test suites, refines them by attributing agent failures to specification defects, and generates single-requirement mutants, so the benchmark can be extended; and an evaluation of six coding agents showing they can implement specifications they cannot test (§1, "Key Contributions") [AP].

## Part II: Constructing TestSuiteBench

The construction runs in three conceptual steps: a detailed draft specification derived from the reference test suite (§2.1), mutants built from the draft specification and the reference suite so that each is killed by a single test (§2.2), and iterative polishing of the specification to remove ambiguities and contradictions (§2.3) (§2, "Benchmark Construction") [AP]. Figure 2's caption describes the same pipeline and adds that, in the space of implementations, the set of admissible implementations is first defined using T and then aligned with the set the specification S admits (Figure 2 caption) [AP]. Throughout construction the authors use Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol at high reasoning (§2.1, "Generating a Draft Specification") [AP].

### Why not developer documentation

The authors manually inspected developer-written documentation for representative repositories and "found them severely underspecified and thus unsuitable for test generation" (§2.1, "Generating a Draft Specification") [V]. They therefore generate richer specifications suitable for both test and program generation (§2.1, "Generating a Draft Specification") [AP]. Part III records the measured comparison (Table 5).

### Reference implementation and test-suite refinement

The starting point is the 200 instances of ProgramBench (Yang et al., 2026), whose construction the authors summarise: 200 open-source GitHub repositories with compiled standalone executables, primarily Rust, Go or C++; a coding agent built an extensive test suite from each repository's tests and the executable's observed behaviour, with every test a pure input-output behaviour assertion; and the suites were audited manually and automatically for under- or over-specification (§2.1, "Reference Implementation") [BT].

The authors filter out tests that need internet access, need excessive resources, or are flaky on the reference implementation, and drop an instance if filtering shrinks its suite significantly; this leaves 165 instances, whose reference suites shrank by 5.7% on average (§2.1, "Test Suite Refinement") [AE]. Appendix B.1 gives the criteria: a resource limit of 2 CPU cores, 60 GB RAM and 1 hour per test-environment run, with tests failing under it removed; exclusion of repositories whose reference suites need internet access, detected by running the suite without network access; and exclusion of any test that fails on the reference implementation at any step of the pipeline (App. B.1, "Details on Filtering") [AP].

### Draft specification generation

A coding agent writes a semi-structured draft specification S′ that describes every behaviour tested by T∗ explicitly, in at most 50 sections; the draft is later refined to remove ambiguity, contradiction and underspecification with respect to input-output behaviour (§2.1, "Draft Specification Generation") [AP]. The specification-initialization prompt asks the agent to give someone enough information to implement an executable that passes all the tests without relying on anything outside the specification, to title each section "## Spec {i}", to use at least 10 and at most 50 sections by aggregating similar requirements, and to write an abstracted description of expected behaviour rather than enumerating test functions (App. D.1, "Specification-initialization prompt") [AP].

### Mutant construction: choosing targets

The authors treat the mutant set as the core of the benchmark, since the mutants' specificity and diversity determine how well it measures a suite's strength; they aim for targeted changes that break only specific requirements while being otherwise indistinguishable (§2.2, "Mutant Construction") [AR]. For each mutant they pick a target test intended to kill it and aim for no other reference test to kill it (§2.2, "Mutant Construction") [AP].

Because reference suites are large (median 679 tests), they target only a subset of test functions chosen to cover S′ uniformly, and argue that this suffices: "This is sufficient for strong mutation testing, since the later test generation can not know which requirements will be tested by the mutants and thus has to evenly cover the entire specification" (§2.2, "Mutant Construction") [V].

They build a bipartite graph linking each specification section to the test functions that assert its requirements, and pick 6 target tests per section so that each test is selected by as few sections as possible, solved optimally as a min-cost flow problem (§2.2, "Candidate Construction") [AP]. Appendix B.2 gives the formulation: a source α and sink ω, edge capacities u(α, s) = 6, u(s, t) = 1 and u(t, ω) = 1 (so each section gets at most six target tests and each test serves at most one mutant), and cost w(s, t) = d(t), the number of sections linked to t; the min-cost max-flow solution favours section-specific tests over tests shared by many sections, with the test identifier breaking ties (App. B.2, "Optimal Selection of Mutant Targets") [AP].

A separate coding agent then modifies the reference implementation for each target test so that it compiles into a mutant killed by that test through a violation of a specific behaviour in the section, retrying up to three times if the code does not compile (§2.2, "Candidate Construction") [AP].

### Mutant construction: refinement

For each section the authors rank its 6 candidate mutants by whether the target test kills them and by how many other tests kill them, keep the top three, and have a coding agent inspect and refine those candidates to reduce the other tests that kill them (§2.2, "Candidate Refinement") [AP]. They then run the reference suite against the mutants and drop any mutant that the intended test does not kill or that more than 20% of unrelated test functions kill (§2.2, "Candidate Refinement") [AP]. Refinement raised the share of mutants killed exactly by the targeted test from 32.4% to 73.0%, and cut the average share of other tests that kill a mutant from 1.45% to 0.17% (§2.2, "Candidate Refinement") [AE].

The prompts show how the agents were steered. The mutant-suite initialization prompt asks each mutant to violate its assigned rule in the narrowest way that makes its assigned test fail while every other active reference test passes, to leave a [MUTATED] comment, and to avoid detecting the test environment or hard-coding literal strings from the target test (App. D.1, "Mutant-suite initialization prompt") [AP]. It states the intended class of fault: "A mutant must be a rule a re-implementer could plausibly get wrong across all inputs in its class" (App. D.1, "Mutant-suite initialization prompt") [V]. It also forbids wrapper or proxy executables that delegate to the reference and leaves compilation to the script (App. D.1, "Mutant-suite initialization prompt") [AP]. The mutant-polishing prompt asks the agent to make each listed mutant fail its target test while minimising other failures, to preserve the mutation's behavioural topic, and to prefer the smallest source-level change; it states that an exact singleton kill set is desirable but not required (App. D.1, "Mutant-polishing prompt") [AP].

### Specification refinement loop

The draft specifications are refined by an iterative process (§2.3, "Specification Refinement") [AP]:

- *Trial Generations.* Two coding agents generate an implementation Î and a test suite T̂ from S′; Î is run against the reference tests, and T̂ against the reference executable and the mutant set (§2.3, "Trial Generations") [AP].
- *Error Attribution.* Each failure (a reference test killing Î, a generated test killing I∗, or a mutant surviving T̂) is classified as a bad generation or a defect of S′, either underspecification (ambiguous, insufficient) or contradiction (misleading, wrong) (§2.3, "Error Attribution") [AP].
- *Specification Refinement.* An agent revises the affected sections: contradictions are corrected, and underspecified sections get further detail drawn from the reference tests (§2.3, "Specification Refinement") [AP].

The loop repeats until fewer than 5% of generated-test failures are attributed to the specification (§2.3, "Specification Refinement") [AP]. Figure 3's caption reports that refinement raises the implementations' reference pass rate and the tests' validity rate while the mutation score stays low, and the text notes that the test validity rate in particular rose significantly as ambiguities were clarified (§2.3; Figure 3 caption) [AE].

Appendix D.1 gives three classification prompts for this step. The accuracy-classification prompt attributes candidate-implementation failures on the reference suite to the executable, to specification underspecification or contradiction, to the environment (error), or to unknown (App. D.1, "Accuracy-classification prompt") [AP]. The precision-classification prompt classifies generated tests that failed on the ground-truth executable as the test's fault, a specification fault, an error or unknown, and treats a timing-sensitive test with flaky siblings as a race in the test where the specification describes the behaviour as asynchronous, consolidated or best-effort, unless the reference fails the invocation deterministically on replay (App. D.1, "Precision-classification prompt") [AP]. The recall-classification prompt classifies survived mutants as specification faults, as the generated suite's weakness ("test"), or unknown, and forbids recommending any change to a mutant (App. D.1, "Recall-classification prompt") [AP]. Both the accuracy and precision prompts require a claimed contradiction to quote the specification sentence as a literal substring, and discard the verdict if the quote is not found (App. D.1, "Accuracy-classification prompt"; "Precision-classification prompt") [AP]. The evaluation prompts in D.2 also serve as the mock-run step of this loop (App. D.2, "Evaluation") [AP].

### Manual quality control

The authors check the resulting specifications, mutants and reference suites by hand and fix minor issues, such as tests inherited from ProgramBench that expect crashes at specific source lines; 34 instances needed such intervention (§2.4, "Manual Quality Control") [AE]. In 20 instances the specification contained a specific error location, such as stdout including a panic at a given line of src/main.rs, which let every mutant be killed by a single test because the location differs per mutant; they replaced it with an obfuscated placeholder and removed tests that check that property (App. B.3, "Findings in Manual Quality Check") [AE]. In 14 instances the specification described behaviours tied to tests flagged to be skipped, such as tests needing the internet, and those behaviours were dropped (App. B.3, "Findings in Manual Quality Check") [AE].

### The finished benchmark

The benchmark has 165 instances in Rust, Go and C/C++, spanning domains including text processing, file and disk utilities, and build tools (§2.5, "TestSuiteBench") [AE]. Figure 4 gives the language split as Rust 97 (59%), Go 41 (25%), C/C++ 26 (16%) and Other 1 (1%) (Figure 4) [AE]. Specifications have a median of about 5k words across 23 sections; instances have a median of 679 reference test functions and 67 mutants; reference implementations range from 538 to 1.6M lines of code, median 7k (§2.5, "TestSuiteBench"; Table 1) [AE]. Table 7 lists all 165 repositories with their section, mutant and reference-test counts (App. E, "List of Instances") [AP].

| Table 1 statistic | Min | Max | Median |
|---|---|---|---|
| S: words | 2,065 | 27,406 | 5,635 |
| S: lines | 158 | 3,258 | 576 |
| S: sections | 10 | 50 | 23 |
| S: files | 1 | 46 | 1 |
| I: lines of code | 538 | 1,613,380 | 7,008 |
| T: test functions | 85 | 13,298 | 679 |
| M: mutants | 27 | 148 | 67 |

Source: Table 1, column alignment checked against `pdftotext -layout` [AE].

### Evaluation metrics

A generated suite T̂ gets two scores (§2.6, "Evaluation Metrics") [AP]:

- **Mutation Score (M):** the fraction of mutants killed by T̂. Tests that fail on the reference executable are filtered out before M is computed, because tests that kill every executable would inflate it; suites are run 3 times on the reference executable and tests whose behaviour changes across runs are removed (§2.6, "Evaluation Metrics") [AP].
- **Validity Rate (V):** the fraction of generated tests that do not kill the reference executable (§2.6, "Evaluation Metrics") [AP]. Figure 1 calls it the Validity Score, and §1 and §3.1 call it the validity score (Figure 1 caption; §1, "Our work"; §3.1, "Agents Generate Valid Tests and Implementations", "Valid but Weak Tests") [AP].

A generated implementation Î is scored by its **Reference Pass Rate (R)**, the fraction of reference tests that do not kill it (§2.6, "Evaluation Metrics") [AP]. To prevent cheating, agents run in Docker containers without networking and with CLI search tools disabled, but with standard libraries and the reference implementation's dependencies pre-installed (§2.6, "Evaluation Metrics") [AP].

Appendix C adds that M is the primary focus, and that the test-generation prompt explicitly tells agents that tests failing on the reference are excluded from M and asks them to break suites into smaller, focused tests so that a partly failing test does not remove a large gradable part (App. C, "Evaluation") [AP].

## Part III: Experimental results

### Models and setup

The agents use GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, Gemini-3.8 Flash and DeepSeek V4 Flash, at default reasoning effort unless stated and with vendor-recommended harnesses, under a 6-hour timeout (§3, "Models and Setup") [AP]. Appendix C names the harnesses as Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI and DeepSeek Harness; each model runs in a container with 2 CPUs and 256 GB RAM and a 6-hour limit per instance, for code generation and for test generation separately (App. C, "Models and Agent Harnesses") [AP].

Code and test generation share one container per task, pre-installed with the libraries the reference implementation and tests use, with the internet disabled except for the API provider's endpoint (App. C, "Solution Generation") [AP]. For code generation, following ProgramBench, the agent writes a build script that produces an executable, and the tests check the executable's behaviour, which allows language-agnostic grading (App. C, "Solution Generation") [AP]. Test suites must report results as JUnit XML; because models struggled to generate the XML themselves, the authors hinted that pytest can produce it, after which all observed submissions used pytest (App. C, "Solution Generation") [AE]. Each code-test pair is evaluated in a separate container with 2 CPUs and 60 GB RAM and no internet (App. C, "Evaluation") [AP].

The test-generation prompt tells the agent that the suite will go through mutation testing and that the specification is available only while authoring, and asks it to cover documented behaviour thoroughly: "The test suite must kill any mutants that go against the spec, while it has to pass any implementation as long as it follows the spec" (App. D.2, "Test-generation prompt") [V]. It also asks for at least one meaningful test per documented behaviour, with particular attention to numbered or sectioned requirements (App. D.2, "Test-generation prompt") [AP]. The code-generation prompt asks the agent to reimplement a new, original codebase from scratch from the specification, without internet search, repository cloning or package downloads, keeping only a self-contained executable (App. D.2, "Code-generation prompt") [AP].

### Main results

Table 2's caption reads: "Frontier agents struggle to achieve M beyond 56%, even when V and R are almost 100%" (Table 2 caption) [V]. Values below are percentages except cost and time; M, V, cost and time sit under the table's "Test Generation" heading, and R is the reference pass rate of the same agents' implementations (Table 2; §3.1, "Agents Struggle to Generate Strong Tests") [AE].

| Model | M | V | $ per instance | t (min) | R |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Opus 5 | 55.5 | 96.1 | 10.56 | 37.0 | 91.8 |
| GPT 6 Astra | 50.1 | 94.3 | 2.18 | 12.4 | 92.7 |
| Gemini 3.8 Flash | 37.9 | 88.2 | 1.63 | 9.3 | 86.2 |
| GPT 5.6 Sol | 37.7 | 94.4 | 0.89 | 8.2 | 86.9 |
| DeepSeek V4 Flash | 28.6 | 78.1 | 0.14 | 19.0 | 66.8 |
| GPT 5.6 Luna | 19.3 | 74.1 | 0.03 | 4.0 | 65.4 |

Source: Table 2, column alignment checked against `pdftotext -layout` [AE].

Claude Opus 5 scores highest at 55.5%, at $10.56 per instance and 37 minutes on average; GPT 6 Astra follows at 50.1% for $2.18 and 12.4 minutes; all other agents score below 40% (§3.1, "Agents Struggle to Generate Strong Tests") [AE]. The abstract summarises the same results as mutation scores below 60%, with 88% of generated tests passing on the reference implementation and implementations for the same specifications passing 82% of reference tests (Abstract) [AE]; the introduction gives the 88% as an average (§1, "Introduction") [AE].

### Valid tests, valid implementations, weak suites

All agents except DeepSeek V4 Flash and GPT 5.6 Luna produce tests with V between 88% and 96% and implementations with R between 86% and 93% (§3.1, "Agents Generate Valid Tests and Implementations") [AE]. The authors read both numbers as showing that the specification is clear and precise enough to convey the expected behaviour, which they take as validating their construction process, and read the high R as showing the specification covers every requirement in enough detail to pass the reference suite (§3.1, "Agents Generate Valid Tests and Implementations") [AR]. "This makes it all the more surprising that all models still fail at generating strong test suites and points to a gap in their capabilities" (§3.1, "Agents Generate Valid Tests and Implementations") [V].

The authors see a concerning implication for practitioners in the gap between V (88-96%) and M (38-56%) (§3.1, "Valid but Weak Tests") [AR]:

> "While the models
> are capable of writing valid tests, giving the impression of well tested software, they fail to write
> discriminative tests that would actually surface specification violations." (§3.1, "Valid but Weak Tests") [V]

They argue this directly limits current agents for autonomous software engineering, and that it reflects commonly observed patterns of code agents writing large test suites yet not detecting failures in their implementations; no citation is given for those patterns (§3.1, "Valid but Weak Tests") [AR].

### Cost, strength and reasoning effort

The authors observe a clear logarithmic relationship between cost and M, with more recent frontier models doing best at the highest prices, and every evaluated model except Gemini 3.8 Flash on the Pareto frontier (§3.1, "Cost-Strength Tradeoff") [AE]. Figure 5's caption puts it as increased cost providing marginal gains for M (Figure 5 caption) [AE]. Varying reasoning effort for GPT 5.6 Sol shows the same trend: M rises from 31.3% at $0.45 per instance on low effort to 46.5% at $2.4 per instance on xhigh (§3.1, "Reasoning Effort") [AE]. Figure 5 plots Sol at low, medium, high and xhigh effort alongside the other agents (Figure 5) [AE].

### Suite size

All models generate smaller suites than the reference in expectation; the gap is smallest for Opus (Δ = −8.9%), and Sol's suites are about 5x smaller than the reference (Δ = −79.9%) (§3.2, "Model Test Suites are (Too) Small"; Figure 6a) [AE]. The authors call this correlation unsurprising, arguing that a high M hinges on covering all requirements exhaustively, which generally takes many tests (§3.2, "Model Test Suites are (Too) Small") [AR]. They observe a general trend of better M where instances have fewer reference tests (and so fewer requirements to cover) and where agents generate more tests (§3.2, "Model Test Suites are (Too) Small") [AE]. Figure 6a's legend gives correlations between reference and generated test counts of ρ = 0.69 for Opus and ρ = 0.27 for Sol, and its caption says Opus generates more tests than Sol with stronger correlation to the reference test count (Figure 6 caption and legend) [AE]. Appendix A.1 extends this to four models (Sol, Gemini, Opus, DeepSeek) and notes Opus as the exception that generates about as many tests as the reference suite (App. A.1, "Correlation between Reference and Generated Test Suite"; Figure 8) [AE].

### Specification length

M correlates negatively with the number of specification sections (Opus ρ = −0.16, Sol ρ = −0.42) (§3.2, "Agents Struggle with Large Specifications"; Figure 6b) [AE]. The authors read this as models struggling to write strong suites for large requirement sets (§3.2, "Agents Struggle with Large Specifications") [AR]. Appendix A.2 describes the correlation across all four plotted agents as weak and negative (App. A.2, "Correlation between Spec Length and Mutation Score"; Figure 9) [AE].

### Executables and mutants built during test generation

Some agents built implementations and mutants to help them write tests without being told to (§3.2, "Executable/Mutant Creation during Test Generation") [AE]. A rule-based parser over the test-generation trajectories detected code-generation attempts (such as writing an executable) and mutation attempts (such as a shell action mentioning mutation) (§3.2, "Executable/Mutant Creation during Test Generation") [AP]. Table 3 reports, for four of the six agents, the number of instances with each kind of attempt (Table 3) [AE]:

| Model | Exec. | Mutants | M |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opus | 149 | 33 | 55.5 |
| Gemini | 102 | 12 | 37.9 |
| Sol | 4 | 0 | 37.7 |
| DeepSeek | 58 | 4 | 28.6 |

Opus creates both most often, which agrees with its M; the Table 3 caption says this could explain its highest M (§3.2; Table 3 caption) [AR]. Even Opus creates mutants in only 33 of 165 instances, which the authors read as potential for mutant-based test-generation methods (§3.2, "Executable/Mutant Creation during Test Generation") [AR]. Sol creates by far the fewest executables and no mutants, yet still scores above DeepSeek (§3.2, "Executable/Mutant Creation during Test Generation"; Table 3) [AE]. From this the authors argue that mutant and executable creation do not seem necessary for strong suites, and that skipping them lets Sol finish suites in far fewer steps than any other model (§3.2, "Executable/Mutant Creation during Test Generation"; Figure 10) [AR].

### Error analysis: what weak suites miss

Figure 7 shows a mutant from the ast-grep instance: the specification says `run`, the pattern-search command, accepts multiple files, and the mutant ignores the second file, b.js. The Opus suite tests `run` with two files and kills the mutant; the Sol suite tests `run` with a single file and misses it (§3.2, "Error Analysis"; Figure 7 caption) [AE]. The authors generalise: "We observe this to be a common pattern where core functionality is tested but input combinations and edge cases are omitted from test suites" (§3.2, "Error Analysis") [V].

Appendix A.6 adds three more mutants (App. A.6, "More Error Analysis"; Figure 14) [AE]:

- *cmatrix, all-bold mode.* The specification requires `-B` to render all rain characters in bold; the mutant aborts after parsing when all-bold mode is selected. Opus starts the renderer with `-B` and detects the failure; Sol's comparable test uses `-a -b -r`, which selects occasional bold rather than all-bold.
- *ast-grep, JavaScript await.* The mutant ignores JavaScript `await` expressions when `run` gets no path and searches the current directory. Opus tests `await` only in Python and nested JavaScript only with another pattern, each on an explicit file; Sol never tests `await`. Both suites miss it.
- *ast-grep, Elvish completions.* The mutant emits a Zsh completion script when Elvish is requested. Opus requests Elvish completions but checks only that the script is long and mentions commands, which the Zsh script still passes; Sol tests completion help and failed shell inference without validating an Elvish script. Both suites miss it.

### Giving the agent the reference executable

To test whether remaining specification ambiguity explains low scores, the authors gave GPT 5.6 Sol the reference executable as well as the specification (§3.2, "Providing Reference Executables for Test Generation") [AE]. V rose from 94.4% to 98.4%, as the model could inspect the executable, but M barely moved, from 37.7% to 38.1% (Table 4) [AE]. "This indicates that a lack of clarity in the specification that could make the model hesitate to add invalid tests does not explain the low mutation scores observed across this analysis" (§3.2, "Providing Reference Executables for Test Generation") [V]. This ablation was run on GPT 5.6 Sol only (Table 4 caption) [AP].

### Developer documentation instead of the benchmark specification

On a subsample of 30 instances that have extensive developer documentation beyond the README, replacing the benchmark's specifications with that documentation drops Sol's M from 25.5% to 4.0% (Table 5) [AE]. Sol writes 40% fewer tests (2,274 against 3,789), and fewer of them are valid (75.4% against 86.7%) (§3.2, "Comparison with Developer-Written Documentation") [AE]. Classifying the failing tests as in §2.3, the original documentation induces three times as many underspecification failures per test (§3.2, "Comparison with Developer-Written Documentation") [AE].

### Overlap of killed mutants

For Opus, Sol and Gemini, out of 12,130 mutants only 3,080 (25%) are killed by all three, and the two weaker models each kill over 200 mutants that neither other model kills (App. A.5, "Overlap of Killed Mutants"; Figure 12) [AE]. Pooling the three suites raises the killed count from 6,584 (54%) for Opus alone to 7,134 (59%), leaving 4,996 (41%) that no model kills (App. A.5, "Overlap of Killed Mutants") [AE]. The authors conclude: "Combining agents thus yields only modest gains" and leave better ways of combining agents to future work (App. A.5, "Overlap of Killed Mutants") [V].

### Realism of the mutants

Selecting mutants killed by a single reference test risks unrealistically niche mutants, for example ones that fail only on a specific input string used in a parametrised test; the authors mitigate this by instructing the mutation agent to mutate the logic (App. A.5, "Realism of the Mutation") [AR]. To show the effect, Figure 13 sets two pairs of mutants side by side, each pair generated for the same target test with and without the instruction; all four are killed only by their target test, so the single-test criterion cannot tell them apart (App. A.5, "Realism of the Mutation"; Figure 13 caption) [AE]. Without the instruction, the agent copies concrete values from the test into the mutant: the hostctl mutant fails only for the domains site1.test, site2.test and site3.test, and the Skeema mutant exits early only for host=localhost:3307 and port=3308, so changing those literals makes each behave like the reference (App. A.5, "Realism of the Mutation") [AE]. With the instruction, the hostctl mutant drops all but the first of three domains whatever their names, and the Skeema mutant lets the separate port override any conflicting port in the host name (App. A.5, "Realism of the Mutation") [AE]. The appendix reports this ablation through these two example pairs (App. A.5, "Realism of the Mutation"; Figure 13) [AP].

### Score distributions and tool use

Figure 10 shows cumulative distributions of R, V and M and of cost, time and step counts for code and test generation, for Sol, Gemini, Opus and DeepSeek (App. A.3, "Score and Cost Distribution"; Figure 10 caption) [AE]. Classifying agent actions as read, search, write, execute or other, the first few steps are dominated by read and search and most later steps by write and execute; write dominates overall, with 60% of Opus's actions being writes (App. A.4, "Tool Use over Trajectories"; Figure 11) [AE]. The authors read this as the model digesting the specification (usually a single file) within a few steps, then writing code and executing it to check its correctness (App. A.4, "Tool Use over Trajectories") [AR].

## Part IV: Positioning, limits and disclosure

### Related work

Among repository-level coding benchmarks, NL2Repo-Bench (Ding et al., 2025) gives agents an extremely detailed specification and ProgramBench (Yang et al., 2026) a reference executable, and both ask the agent to (re)implement the program; TestSuiteBench instead measures test-suite generation from the specification alone (§4, "Repository-Level Coding Benchmarks") [BT].

Among test-generation benchmarks the authors describe SWT-Bench (Mündler et al., 2024), regression tests reproducing user-reported bugs; SWE-Mutation (Sun et al., 2026), issue-directed test generation and program repair using bug reproduction and mutation testing; TestGenEval (Jain et al., 2025), tests for individual source files, measuring validity, coverage and mutation scores; MultiFileTest (Wang et al., 2026), test generation from source for 59 released projects from 21 repositories in Python, Java and JavaScript, mainly by direct prompting and error-fixing loops, plus a four-project agent case study; and RESTestBench (Kogler et al., 2026), individual tests for specified scenarios against three REST services with manually built mutants (§4, "Test Generation Benchmarks") [BT].

They name two differences: prior work generally gives access to an implementation or executable, and restricts test generation to specific behaviours, individual files or concrete issues, so its reference suite size per task, and the expected size of generated suites, is orders of magnitude smaller (§4, "Test Generation Benchmarks"; Table 6) [AR]. Table 6, checked against `pdftotext -layout`, records (Table 6) [AE]:

| Benchmark | # Repos. | Scope | Inputs | \|T\|/N | M | V | Agents |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SWT-Bench | 12 | Issue | I | 3 | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ |
| TestGenEval | 11 | File | I | 57 | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ |
| MultiFileTest | 21 | Few-File | I | – | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ |
| SWE-Mutation | 53 | Issue | I | 62 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| RESTestBench | 3 | Scenario | S, E | 1 | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ |
| TestSuiteBench | 165 | Repository | S | 944 | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

### Limitations the authors state

- *Mutants as a proxy for test strength.* Mutants target a sample of requirements chosen uniformly across the specification, so gaps in untargeted requirements go unpenalised; because agents cannot know which are targeted, the authors argue, "only suites covering the whole specification achieve a high expected score" (§5, "Mutants as a Proxy for Test Strength") [V]. Selecting mutants killed by a single test risks favouring mutants triggered only by that test's exact inputs, mitigated by the logic-level instruction and by removing hard-coded mutants in a manual and agentic audit (§5, "Mutants as a Proxy for Test Strength") [AP]. And "each mutant violates a single requirement by design and need not reflect the distribution of real-world faults" (§5, "Mutants as a Proxy for Test Strength") [V].
- *Specification realism.* The specifications are far more detailed than typical developer documentation; Table 5 measures the difference for GPT 5.6 Sol on 30 instances as 4.0% M with developer documentation against 25.5% with the benchmark's specifications; the authors argue that specifications sufficient to build software from scratch, such as product requirement documents, must be similarly detailed, "making ours a reasonable proxy for this setting" (§5, "Specification Realism") [V]. They add that such detailed specifications may be a more favourable condition than practice offers, "suggesting that our evaluation may still overestimate agents’ test-generation performance" (§5, "Specification Realism") [V].
- *Reference behaviour as ground truth.* Specifications, reference tests and mutants are all aligned with the reference implementation and inherit its bugs and incidental behaviour; obvious cases such as crashes expected at specific source lines were removed by hand, but subtler ones may persist (§5, "Reference Behavior as Ground Truth") [AP]. "We accept this trade-off, as grounding all artifacts in an existing implementation is what makes our construction scale" (§5, "Reference Behavior as Ground Truth") [V].
- *Scope.* Building on ProgramBench limits the benchmark to command-line applications in compiled languages, because ProgramBench gives agents the reference executable, which would expose source code for interpreted languages; since TestSuiteBench provides only the specification, the authors say the pipeline can be extended to interpreted languages such as Python and TypeScript in future work (§5, "Scope") [AP].

### Conclusion

The conclusion restates the finding that frontier agents can build software they cannot verify: their tests are largely valid and their implementations pass most reference tests, yet even the strongest agent's suites kill just over half the mutants (§6, "Conclusion") [AR]. It restates the reference-executable result: "Giving agents the reference executable leaves mutation scores unchanged, pointing to test design rather than specification quality as the bottleneck" (§6, "Conclusion") [V]; the experiment behind it used GPT 5.6 Sol (Table 4) [AP]. Closing this gap, the authors argue, is a prerequisite for fully autonomous development of new software, and the benchmark makes progress toward it measurable (§6, "Conclusion") [AR].

### Reproducibility and AI-usage statements

Section 2 and Section 3 describe construction and evaluation, Appendix D gives the full prompts, and the full benchmark data and reproduction code "will be released upon publication" (Reproducibility Statement) [V]. The title page names testsuitebench.com and eth-sri/testsuitebench (front matter) [AP].

The AI usage statement says coding agents (Codex with GPT-5.6 Sol) constructed and refined the benchmark's reference test suites, specifications and mutants, and that generative AI was also used to create and modify figures, draft parts of the paper and polish the writing (AI Usage Statement) [AP]. It says generative AI was not used to develop conceptual frameworks, propose or refine hypotheses, design or give feedback on methodology or experiments, implement methods, or interpret results; agent-built artefacts were validated by the pipeline's automated checks and the manual quality check, and all AI-assisted text and figures were reviewed and edited by the authors, who take responsibility for the content (AI Usage Statement) [AP].

## Connections the author makes in the text

- ProgramBench (Yang et al., 2026): the base the benchmark builds on, supplying its 200 starting instances, reference executables and test suites, and the build-script approach to code generation; built on, and also contrasted, since it asks agents to re-implement programs given a reference executable [BT] (§2.1, "Reference Implementation"; §4; §5, "Scope"; App. C).
- Carlini (2026) and Lin (2026): cited for agent re-implementations of a C compiler and a web browser; Carlini is also cited for the claim that autonomous development depends on strong verification [BT] (§1, "Introduction").
- Yang et al. (2024), Mürtz & Müller (2025), Huang et al. (2026): cited neutrally for agents' progression from isolated issues to use across the software lifecycle [BT] (§1, "Introduction").
- Jimenez et al. (2024), Deng et al. (2025), Ding et al. (2025), Lu et al. (2025), Vero et al. (2025): cited neutrally as code-generation benchmarks that scaled from issues to complete applications; NL2Repo-Bench (Ding et al., 2025) is contrasted for asking agents to implement from a detailed specification [BT] (§1, "Introduction"; §4).
- SWT-Bench (Mündler et al., 2024), SWE-Mutation (Sun et al., 2026), TestGenEval (Jain et al., 2025), MultiFileTest (Wang et al., 2026), RESTestBench (Kogler et al., 2026): prior test-generation benchmarks, described and contrasted on scope and inputs [BT] (§1, "Introduction"; §4; Table 6).
- Mustafa et al. (2021): cited for natural-language ambiguity, inconsistency and incompleteness as a main source of software testing errors [BT] (§1, "Introduction").
- Jia & Harman (2011): cited for generic rule-based mutations not guaranteeing requirement-specific faults [BT] (§1, "Introduction").
- OpenAI (2026a, 2026b), Anthropic (2026), Google DeepMind (2026), DeepSeek-AI et al. (2026): the GPT-5.6, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 system cards, the Gemini 3.8 Flash model card and the DeepSeek-V4 arXiv preprint, cited neutrally to identify the evaluated models; OpenAI (2026a) is also cited for the GPT-5.6 Sol model used in construction [BT] (§2.1, "Generating a Draft Specification"; §3, "Models and Setup"; App. C; References).

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Re-implementation successes as evidence that autonomous development of new software is within reach.* The authors voice this suggestion and then qualify it: re-implementations can verify against existing tests and reference implementations, which genuinely new software lacks, so until agents can turn specifications into strong test suites, autonomous development of new software remains out of reach (§1, "Introduction"; §6, "Conclusion").
- *Valid tests as a sign of well-tested software.* Valid tests give "the impression of well tested software" while failing to surface specification violations; the authors set the validity-mutation gap against reading validity as strength (§3.1, "Valid but Weak Tests").
- *Specification ambiguity as the explanation for low mutation scores.* The authors argue against it: high V and R, and an unchanged M when Sol was also given the reference executable, point to test design rather than specification precision (§1, "Introduction"; §3.2, "Providing Reference Executables for Test Generation"; §6, "Conclusion").
- *Developer-written documentation as the specification for test generation.* Rejected as severely underspecified, and measured on 30 instances, where Sol's M falls from 25.5% to 4.0% (§2.1, "Generating a Draft Specification"; §3.2, "Comparison with Developer-Written Documentation").
- *Generic rule-based mutations as a guarantee of requirement-specific faults.* The authors say that measuring a suite's strength requires faults violating specific requirements, which generic rule-based mutations cannot guarantee (§1, "Introduction").
- *Test-generation benchmarks scoped to issues, files or scenarios, with the implementation provided.* The authors position the benchmark against these on both counts (§1, "Introduction"; §4, "Test Generation Benchmarks"; Table 6).

## Citation and source-integrity notes

**Coverage.** Complete. The tape (`sources/converted/egashira-testsuitebench-2026.md`, 2,860 lines, 13,308 words, markitdown 0.1.5 from the 25-page arXiv PDF) was read in full, front matter through Table 7; every section, appendix and prompt enumerated in the Structure block was read. The PDF's and tape's SHA-256 hashes match the acquisition manifest.

**Status.** Preprint, arXiv:2610.13065v1 [cs.SE], 9 Oct 2026. The paper does not state peer review. The benchmark data and code are announced for release upon publication, so no repository was read for this reference.

**Tables checked against the PDF.** markitdown scrambled the column order of Tables 1, 2, 3, 6 and 7. Tables 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 and the Figure 4 values were checked against `pdftotext -layout` output of the PDF, and the values above follow that alignment. Table 7's per-instance rows are readable only from the layout text; this reference cites Table 7 for its scope (all 165 instances), not for individual rows.

**Figures.** All 14 figure captions are present in the tape. Figure bodies arrive as run-together axis and label text (Figures 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8-12) or as code listings (Figures 2, 7, 13, 14). In Figures 7 and 14 the tape repeats each specification line twice, a rendering artefact. Figure 12's region counts (114, 214, 222, 782, 926, 1,796, 3,080, and 4,996 "None") appear in the tape without region labels; this reference uses only the counts stated in the A.5 text. The image files themselves are for the orchestrator's image inspection.

**Terms and notation kept from the source.** The source uses ρ in the §3.2 text and r in the Figure 6b legend for the same specification-length correlations; this reference uses the text's ρ. It calls V both "Validity Rate" (§2.6, App. C) and "Validity Score" or "validity score" (Figure 1 caption; §1, "Our work"; §3.1). Its setup cross-references point to §2.5 (§3) and §2.1 (App. C) for the metrics material, which sits in §2.6. Appendix C says code-generation agents write a `build.sh`, while the D.2 code-generation prompt asks for `./compile.sh`. §2.1 describes filtering out tests that need internet access, and App. B.1 describes excluding repositories whose suites need it. The abstract's 82% implementation figure is not restated in the body. Model names are given as the paper gives them.

**Citation style.** Section numbers and run-in headings, as in the Citation style line above; the tape carries page numbers only as bare footer digits.

**Audit.** Pass I applied 2026-10-15 (see the stamp at the top); the audit log is in `references/_audit/`.
